endorsements.quote: This continuous oversight helps counter challenges such as “model drift” [ 39 , 40 ], where variations in new data inputs could compromise AI performance.
Initially, the AI operates in “shadow mode,” allowing for safety assessments without affecting clinical decisions.

unlisted_practices: Assess radiology AI value hierarchically across seven efficacy levels (technical, diagnostic accuracy, diagnostic thinking, therapeutic, patient outcome, cost-effectiveness, local efficacy) before and during implementation.
Conduct budget impact analysis of locally estimated costs, including acquisition, maintenance, training, and workflow adaptation, and who bears costs and benefits, before acquiring AI.
Use multi-criteria decision analysis with local stakeholders to weigh clinical, economic, legal, social, and ethical criteria in AI acquisition decisions.
Evaluate AI with randomized controlled trials or cohort studies to assess impact on diagnostic thinking, therapeutic decisions, and patient outcomes.
Conduct health economic evaluations (cost-effectiveness or cost-utility analysis) of AI systems.

screen.reason: The paper introduces the Radiology AI Deployment and Assessment Rubric (RADAR), a conceptual framework providing recommendations and a hierarchical methodology for evaluating and deploying AI in radiology.
